input: In this tutorial, we will explore the fascinating concept of phase equilibrium as it applies to a partially miscible liquid pair, and by the end you will have a solid understanding of what equilibrium means in this context, what remains fixed when the amounts change, and what shifts when the temperature changes. Partial miscibility is a situation in which two liquids dissolve in one another only up to a certain limit, beyond which the mixture can no longer remain as a single homogeneous phase. When that limit is exceeded, the mixture splits into two distinct liquid phases, one of which is rich in the first liquid while the other is rich in the second liquid, creating a layered system with a visible boundary. At the heart of the matter lies the equilibrium condition, which can be stated in words as the equality of chemical potential across the phases: for each component, the chemical potential in one phase must be equal to the chemical potential in the other phase. Chemical potential can be thought of as the driving force for the movement of matter, in much the same way that a temperature difference drives the flow of heat, and movement continues as long as a difference persists, coming to a halt only when equality is achieved. It is worth noting, however, that this analogy has its limits, since chemical potential depends on composition as well as temperature, meaning that a component can in some circumstances move against its own concentration difference. Provided the temperature and pressure are held fixed, the compositions of the two phases remain fixed as well, and adding more of one liquid simply changes the relative amounts of the two phases rather than their compositions, with the growing phase expanding at the expense of the other. When the temperature is changed, by contrast, the mutual solubility of the pair shifts, the compositions of the phases move accordingly, and at a sufficiently high or low temperature the two phases may merge back into a single phase once again. Ultimately, equilibrium at any temperature means exactly the same thing: the chemical potentials of each component are equal in every phase in which that component is present.
target: Phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair is the condition in which two liquid phases sit side by side and neither changes. By the end of this passage you can state the equilibrium condition in words, say what stays fixed when more of one liquid is added, and say what changes when the temperature changes. Two liquids are partially miscible when each dissolves in the other only up to a limit. Past that limit, the mixture separates into two liquid phases, one rich in the first liquid and the other rich in the second. The equilibrium condition is equality of chemical potential across the phases: for each component, the chemical potential in one phase equals the chemical potential in the other phase. A component moves between phases while its chemical potential differs between them, and the movement stops when the two values meet. Chemical potential plays the part for matter that temperature plays for heat: matter moves down a chemical-potential difference as heat moves down a temperature difference, and movement in either case stops at equality. The analogy stops there, because chemical potential depends on composition as well as temperature, and a component can move against its own concentration difference when the composition of the receiving phase pulls the other way. At fixed temperature and pressure, the compositions of the two phases are fixed. Adding more of one liquid changes the amounts of the two phases, not their compositions: the phase rich in that liquid grows at the expense of the other, and the overall composition fixes the proportions in which the phases stand. Temperature changes the picture itself. The mutual solubility of the pair shifts with temperature, the two phase compositions move, and at a high enough or low enough temperature the phases merge into one. A partially miscible pair is described by the compositions of its two phases at each temperature, and equilibrium at any temperature means the same thing: equality of chemical potential for each component across the phases present.
